writing.title: 3 things I learned reading Deep Work
writing.subtitle: Cal Newport’s rules for focused success in a distracted world
writing.excerpt: Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University. He received a Ph.D. in computer science from MIT in 2009 and worked as a post-doctoral associate researching…
writing.html:
Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University. He received a Ph.D. in computer science from MIT in 2009 and worked as a post-doctoral associate researching distributed algorithms until 2011, when he joined Georgetown.

Beyond academic papers, Newport also wrote many books about productivity and attention management in the digital world, like Slow Productivity (2024), A World Without Email (2021), Digital Minimalism (2019), Deep Work (2016), and So Good They Can't Ignore You (2012).

Honestly, I'm a big fan of his work. I also studied computer science, so I share his passion for dissecting algorithms, and I've spent a good part of my career reflecting on how to be productive. In the last three years I've been working on building data and business intelligence systems in the advertising industry. It's a naturally creative, chaotic, and media-oriented industry, so I have to deal with a lot of distractions every day.

Newport's books have helped me a lot so far. I started with Slow Productivity. It guided me to calm down my productivity anxiety and really think about the things that matter in my day. I thought it was a good book with good insights. Then I read Deep Work. It was something else.

Since I finished reading Deep Work, a couple of weeks ago, I've noticed a profound impact on my behavior and the way I deal with distraction. Three things happened:

(1) I became aware of mindless Internet consumption. I reduced the use of social media, instant messaging, and streaming apps.

(2) I started hearing my own thoughts. Whenever I'm commuting, running, or grocery shopping, there is no Internet stimulus anymore. The podcast in the background was replaced by a voice in my head that helps me develop my thoughts.

(3) I incorporated writing as part of my thinking. I'm not just writing for a blog or newsletter anymore. I'm writing to think. Writing became a way to record the conversations I have in my head and document my thoughts in a personal knowledge system.

I'll dive deeper and explain how each of these things happened. Let's start with number one.

I became aware of mindless Internet consumption

Before reading Deep Work, my typical workday would go like this: wake up and check my Instagram feed for half an hour in bed; cook breakfast listening to a Spotify playlist; walk to work listening to a podcast on Spotify; alternate between meetings and checking my LinkedIn feed; walk back home listening to a YouTube monologue; exercise while listening to another Spotify playlist; and spend the rest of the day watching series with my wife on Netflix, Apple TV, Amazon Prime Video, or Disney+.

I thought this was normal. After all, that's how most people I know behave. Looking back at my screen time from a couple of weeks ago, I clocked four hours on my phone, received eighty notifications, and picked it up sixty times every day, on average.

Again, for most people this is what routine looks like: we work eight hours, sleep eight hours, and spend the rest of the day trying to entertain our brains with media.

It didn't take long for Newport to convince me I could be doing better things with my time. I could read a book to solve a problem at work. I could read about exercising, eating healthier, and communicating with my partner. I could even write about my learnings and share them with other people. All these ideas seemed nice. But as the chapters passed, I realized that getting time back from media consumption was just the tip of the iceberg.

Newport brings research showing that mindless content consumption also hurts your brain's ability to learn new skills and produce high-quality work. "Constant attention switching online," Newport says, "has a lasting negative effect on your brain (...) People who multitask all the time can't filter out irrelevancy. They can't manage a working memory. They're chronically distracted. They initiate much larger parts of their brain that are irrelevant to the task at hand... they're pretty much mental wrecks."

I genuinely thought I could turn off my phone whenever I needed to focus on my work. Turns out my brain doesn't work this way. According to neuroscientists cited by Newport, when you focus on a single task at a time, the brain develops myelin around neurons, which improves your ability to develop new skills and produce high-quality work. Here is a passage I extracted from the book:

Skills, be they intellectual or physical, eventually reduce down to brain circuits. This new science of performance argues that you get better at a skill as you develop more myelin around the relevant neurons, allowing the corresponding circuit to fire more effortlessly and effectively. To be great at something is to be well myelinated. (...) Why it's important to focus intensely on the task at hand while avoiding distraction is because this is the only way to isolate the relevant neural circuit enough to trigger useful myelination. (...) To learn hard things quickly, you must focus intensely without distraction. To learn, in other words, is an act of deep work.

Once I realized I could have a significant amount of time back as well as improve my ability to learn new things and produce high-quality work just by focusing on single tasks, I deleted all these apps from my phone.

I followed James Clear's advice (Atomic Habits) on how to break bad habits: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult, and unsatisfying. No apps, no media consumption. For a week or two, I was just bored, and then something unexpected happened.

I started hearing my own thoughts

I started hearing a voice in my head, especially in the boring moments, when I was grocery shopping, walking to work, or running on a treadmill with no podcast in the background.

It didn't happen suddenly. It gradually became a thing. I started to hear my thoughts more and more. It became an internal dialogue that I was able to sustain for more than just a couple of minutes.

At first, I followed Newport's advice and embraced boredom. I started taking care of my brain like an athlete takes care of their body. I made a deliberate effort throughout the day to avoid distractions and the dependence on media consumption.

During moments of extreme boredom, I started practicing something Newport calls "productive meditation." I started focusing on a single problem and trying to isolate and analyze its variables. Here is how he explains this method:

The goal of productive meditation is to take a period in which you're occupied physically but not mentally—walking, jogging, driving, showering—and focus your attention on a single well-defined professional problem. Depending on your profession, this problem might be outlining an article, writing a talk, making progress on a proof, or attempting to sharpen a business strategy. As in mindfulness meditation, you must continue to bring your attention back to the problem at hand when it wanders or stalls. I'm not, however, suggesting this practice for its productivity benefits (though they're nice). I'm instead interested in its ability to rapidly improve your ability to think deeply. By forcing you to resist distraction and return your attention repeatedly to a well-defined problem, it helps strengthen your distraction-resisting muscles, and by forcing you to push your focus deeper and deeper on a single problem, it sharpens your concentration. To succeed with productive meditation, it's important to recognize that, like any form of meditation, it requires practice to do well. (...) "Thinking deeply" about a problem seems like a self-evident activity, but in reality it's not. When faced with a distraction-free mental landscape, a hard problem, and time to think, the next steps can become surprisingly non-obvious. In my experience, it helps to have some structure for this deep thinking process. I suggest starting with a careful review of the relevant variables for solving the problem and then storing these values in your working memory. For example, if you're working on the outline for a book chapter, the relevant variables might be the main points you want to make in the chapter.

Practicing productive meditation was the cure for my boredom. I started practicing it to strengthen my mental muscles and my ability to focus. Then it became fun. Every time I saw myself in a boring situation, I told myself, "okay, I'm bored, what am I going to think about now?"

Boring moments like being in an elevator became amusing because I saw people mindlessly scrolling through their feeds while my brain was overflowing with ideas. Setting aside the deep complexity of the mind, I felt like I was in control of my thoughts.

I was now leading the way. I could chat with myself and have long discussions about things I wanted to create and problems I wanted to solve. Then the internal voice became louder and louder. It became so intense that I had to do something about it.

I incorporated writing as part of my thinking

Writing was the only sane thing to do with that voice in my head. I didn't start writing a daily journal. I didn't set a specific goal or routine for writing. I also didn't intend to share any of my writing. I started writing for me, whenever I felt like it, as a part of my thinking process.

That mindset changed my relationship with the act of writing. All my life I used to write with a final product in mind, like an article, a work presentation, or an academic paper. Now I write just to think.

I write during the productive meditation sessions. After about ten minutes analyzing a thought, the impulse to write and document the thought becomes impossible to ignore. In the past few weeks I wrote ten long notes based on my productive meditation sessions. The list couldn't look more random:

  • 2026-10-12, starting a business vs making content: I compared Ali Abdaal's lifestyle business approach (create a high-ticket 1:1 service offer and acquire customers through warm outreach) with Dan Koe's approach (create a micro-product and a micro-service and acquire customers with content and newsletters).

  • 2026-10-14, feeling adrift: I wrote a deep reflection about the fact that I had been feeling adrift since I turned thirty, and how I can try living a fulfilling life by writing about the things I love.

  • 2026-10-16, acronyms ruin communication: I made a point that acronyms should be avoided in business communication as much as possible. I argued that acronyms are ambiguous, confusing, and an ineffective tool for human communication.

  • 2026-10-17, build a business like you're building a village in Clash of Clans: I made an analogy about how building a lifestyle business as an adult compares to building a Clash of Clans village in high school. This one was the most enjoyable to write, if I'm being honest.

  • 2026-10-17, running slower makes it easier to run more: I explained how I transformed my "easy runs" into "think runs." I started to run slower on a treadmill instead of running faster on the streets. I stopped paying attention to pace control and city traffic, and this allowed me to think more deeply during an easy run.

  • 2026-10-19, today I helped my wife set up her second brain: I documented the fact that my wife is starting a new job in the advertising industry as a media buyer and she asked me for advice on how to be a high performer. I used Tiago Forte's Second Brain approach and helped her set up a knowledge system that she can use to ease her onboarding process.

  • 2026-10-19, how a Brazilian ends up immigrating to Canada: I told my story of leaving Brazil, changing careers from lawyer in Brazil to computer scientist in Canada, diving deep into the thought process of why I picked Canada instead of any other country.

  • 2026-10-22, a case for tacit knowledge in AI data agent development: I made an argument that AI data agents need access to tacit knowledge documentation, not just explicit data and instructions, to improve accuracy.

  • 2026-10-22, 3 things I learned reading Deep Work: the text you are reading right now.

  • 2026-10-23, Luhmann vs Ravikant: I made a comparison between how Niklas Luhmann and Naval Ravikant approached their challenges and ended up with an unexpectedly similar philosophy.

When I stop to think about it, that's a lot of long texts I wrote in a short time. Granted, most are only first drafts. Yet I wrote almost one long text per day. Some on the same day. Some a couple of days apart. I could never dream of writing this much before reading Deep Work.

I might use one of these texts for work, a couple more for Substack articles, and leave the others simmering for days, months, or years. I'm sure in the coming days I'll write a lot more. Like I said, writing became just a part of the thinking process. If I'm not writing, it means I'm not thinking. If I'm not thinking, it means I'm not deep working.

Nobel Prize winner Richard Feynman put it this way. He was being interviewed by a historian, who looked at his notebooks and said they were wonderful records of the physicist's thinking. Feynman immediately stopped the historian and said, "They aren't a record of my thinking process. They are my thinking process. I actually did the work on the paper. (...) It's not a record, not really. It's working. You have to work on paper, and this is the paper." (I saw this story about Feynman in How to Make Smart Notes, by Sönke Ahrens. I'll dive deeper into it in the future.)

writing.title: Today I helped my wife set up her second brain
writing.subtitle: She is ready to start a new job as a senior media buyer feeling confident in her skills
writing.excerpt: My wife just got a new job at a big advertising agency as a senior media buyer and she starts next week. Today we were chatting about her onboarding schedule during breakfast and I felt…
writing.html:
My wife just got a new job at a big advertising agency as a senior media buyer and she starts next week. Today we were chatting about her onboarding schedule during breakfast and I felt like her "first day at school" jitters are starting to kick in.

She mentioned feeling insecure about all the new ad platforms she will have to learn and work on. She asked if I had any thoughts on how to onboard smoothly and become a high performer on her team.

Honestly, I'm no performance coach, but I've been working in a big agency for a while. I first joined as a senior data analyst and in the past couple of years I got promoted to analytics manager based on good performance.

I'm also not a media buyer, but I read more productivity books than I can count. From waking up at 4AM, doing daily cold plunges, creating kanban boards, and scheduling pomodoro time blocks, I feel like I've tested a bunch of tools, frameworks, and routines. Some worked well, some didn't (I still wake up at 8AM and take hot showers). But I thought I might be in a good position to share what worked for me.

I opened my toolbox looking for something that might be useful for someone starting a new job. After digging through some notes in my Obsidian vault, I found this one that said: "Knowledge work is about managing information effectively".

This is a useful note for her, I thought. After all, she is a knowledge worker who will have to deal with a ton of new information in her new job. When I opened the note, it said:

"We live in a world where distracted people are overwhelmed by the volume of information they have to manage every day. Managing information effectively is a competitive advantage. You should not waste your time and energy looking for old emails or trying to remember what was said during a meeting that happened weeks ago. Staying late in the office every day searching for files, emails, and presentations is not a sign of success, it's a sign of burnout."

Again, useful context. Starting a new job is overwhelming. There are new people to meet, new processes to learn, new systems to master. If she finds a way to manage information effectively, she will likely become a high performer on her team.

As a bonus, if she manages information effectively, she can be home early instead of staying late in the office wasting time searching through emails, remembering meetings, and making the same presentation for the tenth time.

Now the question is: how can she manage information effectively? This is not mentioned in the note, but might be somewhere near. I kept digging through the connected notes.

The "knowledge work" note was also linked to some useful notes, like "You can't use your head to store all your knowledge", "A note is a unit of knowledge", and "Technology allows your notes to be stored digitally". But none of these notes offered a structured method to help her.

That's when I realized all notes in this neighbourhood had the same root: the book "Building a Second Brain", by Tiago Forte. A couple of links away, I found a note that summarized Tiago's approach to building a second brain.

The note said: "The Second Brain is a personal knowledge management system for capturing notes, organizing in folders, distilling ideas and expressing your creations". When I opened the note, it said:

The "Second Brain" is a personal knowledge management (PKM) system created by Tiago Forte. It can be used for storing notes, connecting ideas, and creating things. It works like a private knowledge collection, a laboratory for new ideas, and a digital garden for cultivating your creations. It is a mind cathedral where you can go alone to think, as well as a repository of things you create.

The Second Brain system follows a process called "CODE", which means Capture, Organize, Distill, and Express. Capture means taking notes about any idea that resonates, based on your intuition. Organize means placing notes where they are more likely to be used, based on a folder hierarchy called "PARA", acronym for Projects, Areas, Resources, and Archive. Distill means getting to the essence of an idea using Progressive Summarization. Express means sharing your work as early as possible and as frequently as possible, to capture feedback from other people.

This is a great note. But it's also a lot to unpack for someone who has never read Tiago's book. So I broke the ideas into three steps to help her set up a second brain:

First, I explained that the second brain is a personal knowledge system that can be implemented in tools like Notion, Evernote, or Obsidian. She was already into Obsidian because I've been using it and telling her how great it is for some time. Obsidian is a free note-taking app, essentially a text editor. It works well on her iPhone and Mac, via iCloud. Also, it integrates easily with Claude for searching notes and doing cleanups. I avoid using Claude for knowledge-related activities (like writing notes, distilling notes, connecting notes), but Claude can be a time saver for admin work. So she went ahead and downloaded Obsidian.

Second, I explained that the second brain is organized in four folders: Projects, Areas, Resources, and Archive. She went ahead and created the folders. She also decided to create one project note called "onboarding" (following the 30-60-90 onboarding approach), one area note called "people" (to store what she knows about her new coworkers), and one resource folder to store study notes for each ad platform she will use (Meta, Snapchat, CM360, DV360, and The Trade Desk). Yes, it's a lot of ad platforms.

Third, I explained that from now on, she will have to keep a habit of capturing notes about projects, people, processes, and ad platforms, for example. She will also have to make sure these notes are organized in the right folders. From time to time she will have to go back to these notes and summarize them, as well as archive the ones that are not useful anymore.

After a couple of hours setting up her second brain in Obsidian, it took her another hour (and a grilled cheese break) to wrap her head around the process of feeding and maintaining the system.

But now she's not looking insecure anymore.

She's looking curious, engaged, and focused on studying ad platform documentation. She's already making some good-looking notes and feeling ready to face a new professional challenge.

notes.title: A note represents a physical unit of knowledge
notes.html:
A note is the representation of an idea in physical form stored in your knowledge system. When you write a note, you are capturing an idea and making it available to your future self. You can write a note about a book chapter, a movie scene, a podcast dialogue, a conversation with a friend, or a journal reflection. "It al begins with the simple act of writing things down." (Forte, 2022)

See:

Tiago Forte - Building a Second Brain

notes.title: Build knowledge outside your brain
notes.html:
Notes are the outcome of the learning process. Reading, thinking, and discussing all happen inside your head. If you don’t take notes along the way, you will end up with all your knowledge stored only inside your brain, with no physical representation.

Brainstorming is basically searching for ideas you collected from outside sources and stored inside your brain. When you “think through writing”, you don’t need to brainstorm, because your ideas are well documented and ready to use.

notes.html:
Creative work happens through collecting references and reorganizing other people’s creations that inspire you.

Artists explain their influences in interviews when asked how they created a movie, a song or a painting. Scientists list their sources at the and of a scientific paper.

“We all stand on the shoulders of giants, and it's smart to build on the thinking they've done rather than try to reinvent the wheel.” (Forte, 2022)

notes.title: Creativity is just connecting things (Steve Jobs, 1996)
notes.html:
In an interview for Wired in 1996, Steve Jobs was asked about why other companies were not able to make well-designed products like Apple did. In that moment, Steve Jobs said that “creativity is just connecting things” and creative people don’t create things, they just see connections between things they experienced and thought through.

“Creativity is just connecting things. When you ask creative people how they did something, they feel a little guilty because they didn’t really do it, they just saw something. It seemed obvious to them after a while. That’s because they were able to connect experiences they’ve had and synthesize new things. And the reason they were able to do that was that they’ve had more experiences or they have thought more about their experiences than other people. (…) A lot of people in our industry haven’t had very diverse experiences. So they don’t have enough dots to connect, and they end up with very linear solutions without a broad perspective on the problem. The broader one’s understanding of the human experience, the better design we will have.“

notes.title: Distill an idea to understand its essence
notes.html:
In the moment you capture a new idea into your knowledge system, you will probably include a lot of context from your source. With time, the idea will get more familiar to you and the context will clutter your notes, making them harder to use in the future.

Think about when you read a book for the first time. When you are surprised with a new idea, you are likely to highlight the concept, the context, and a couple of examples.

Its fine for a literature note to be long. But when you come back to that note in the future, it will take you more than a couple of minutes to remember what its about.

If you keep coming back to that long note, it can be time consuming. That's when you know you need to distill the idea to its smallest understandable version: the essence.

notes.title: Distilling ideas in a knowledge system helps you overcome recency bias
notes.html:
Recency bias is a tendency to overvalue recent information, ideas and experiences. To overcome recency bias, you have to capture an idea and give it some time. Your knowledge system is a great tool to overcome recency bias. There is a natural passage of time between the moment you capture an idea on a literature note to the moment you distill it and write it on a permanent note. Sometimes days, sometimes weeks.

notes.title: Every work of knowledge starts with writing a note
notes.html:
Whether you want to write a book, a scientific paper, an article, or a newsletter, it all starts with the habit of note-taking. When you read every day and write notes about what you read, the notes become raw material for your writing products.

There is a difference between the writing product and the writing process. The writing product is delivered once, but the writing process happens every day.

You should not start writing a paper by staring at a blank page. You should take notes while you are reading. Writing a good note means explaining something you learned to your future self by using your own words. So when it's time to write about a topic, you already have dozens of notes ready to be organized into a final product.

notes.title: Fleeting notes are quick notes you capture in the moment
notes.html:
The fleeting note is just a reminder. The purpose of capturing a fleeting note is to remind you to make a permanent note later.

You could write a fleeting note on a piece of napkin, in a pocket notebook, or store it in the inbox of your note-taking app for later processing.

Once you process the information into a permanent note, you can discard the fleeting note (either throw it away, delete it, or archive it).

If you take too long to process a fleeting note, say more than two days, the information might become vague, confusing, or irrelevant. This can happen if you end up with a lot of unprocessed fleeting notes. They lose their value over time when left unprocessed.

See:

notes.title: Francis Coppola distilled The Godfather novel into a film
notes.html:
When Paramount Studios acquired the rights to The Godfather novel, they offered multiple filmmakers to make a movie about it, but everyone refused because they hated the book.

Francis Coppola refused at first, but his partner George Lucas pressured him into accepting the offer because they needed the money. He had the challenge to make a book everyone hated into a movie that wasn’t so bad.

Francis read the novel, ripped off the pages he liked and stored them in a binder. He broke the whole novel into movie scenes. He refined each scene by writing notes about the context that should be communicated within each scene. He consulted the binder during the entire production of the movie, and the rest is history.

The Godfather Notebook is a great example of distilling an idea to its essence.

notes.title: Literature notes are ideas you capture while reading
notes.html:
The problem with taking notes in the margins of a book and highlighting quotes is: when you close the book, the information is gone with it. It's hard to create a body of knowledge of your own when your notes are scattered and siloed in multiple books.

Instead, you can take literature notes. When you read something valuable in a book, write it down on a literature note, using your own words. Bring quotes if you need, but be selective. Add the source to the note, and store it in your knowledge system.

notes.title: Shift from content consumer to content creator by taking notes
notes.html:
Shift from content consumer to content creator by taking notes.

Develop the habit of saving your favourite content along with a note about why you liked it.

After some time, you will end up with a lot of notes in different stages of maturity. Some notes will be longer; others will be just a phrase.

You can keep consuming endlessly, but at some point your notes will naturally allow you to shift from consuming to creating.

A scarcity mindset will tell you that you need to consume every piece of content in the world about a topic to be able to create content about it.

An abundance mindset shows you need only a handful of notes to start creating.

When you focus on creating content about your favourite topic, all the useful notes will suddenly emerge, and you will be able to write effortlessly.

Any time of the day, she uses her phone to write ideas for hooks, verses, phrases, and record voice memos by humming rhythms and melodies.

notes.title: The Archipelago of Ideas is a writing technique that separates divergent and convergent thinking is different phases
notes.html:
Writing on a blank page can be hard if you try to select the ideas you want to write about and put them in a logical sequence at the same time. Selecting ideas is a divergent task, requires you to explore your notes, and sequencing ideas is a convergent task, that asks you to focus on what’s important.

You can create an Archipelago of Ideas by dropping groups of notes in small islands on a page, so much of your writing is reduced to just building the bridges between them.

notes.title: The creative process alternates between divergent and convergent thinking
notes.html:
Divergent thinking is about exploring new ideas, considering various hypothesis and coming up with multiple solutions. It’s a chaotic process by nature, with the purpose of creating a vast amount of options.

Convergent thinking is about selecting the best options, eliminating the clutter, and making trade-offs. It’s an organized process by nature, with the purpose of focusing on the best solution.

notes.title: The products of creativity are constantly changing, but the creative process is timeless
notes.html:
If you look around, there is always a hot trend in creative products.

As I write this in 2026, the most popular contents consumed are short form videos on Instagram or TikTok. Ten years ago it was live streaming, before that was MP3s and DVDs, in the nineties it was CDs, in the eighties VHS tapes, then vinyl records, newspapers, and a hundred years ago it was AM radio broadcasts. Before that we had creative products that are still around, like literature, paintings, music, architecture, cooking…

The point is creative products change in popularity as society evolves. But if you turn your attention to the creative process behind any of these products, it all comes down to collecting references and connecting ideas to inspire new creations.

notes.title: The Second Brain is a personal knowledge management system for capturing notes, organizing in folders, distilling ideas and expressing your creations
notes.html:
The "Second Brain" is a personal knowledge management (PKM) system created by Tiago Forte. It can be use for storing notes, connecting ideas, and creating things. It works like a private knowledge collection, a laboratory for new ideas, and a digital garden for cultivating your creations. It is a mind cathedral where you can go alone to think, as well as a repository of things you create.

The Second Brain system follows a process called "CODE", which means Capture, Organize, Distill, and Express. Capture means taking notes about any idea that resonates, based on your intuition. Organize means placing notes where they are more likely to be used, based on a folder hierarchy called "PARA", acronym for Projects, Areas, Resources, and Archive. Distill means getting to the essence of an idea using Progressive Summarization. Express means sharing your work as early as possible and as frequently as possible, to capture feedback from other people.

See:

notes.title: The Zettelkasten is a note-based personal knowledge system that represents a network of connected ideas, facts, and mental models
notes.html:
Around the 1960s, the German sociologist Niklas Luhmann came up with a system to organize his notes called the “Zettelkasten”. Zettelkasten can be translated to English as “slip-box”, and its basically a set of wooden boxes that store index cards (A6 format).

Luhmann’s system relied on two slip-boxes, one for collecting literature notes and one for permanent notes.

Whenever Luhmann wrote a note, he added to the slip-box with an identification: a code formed by numbers and letters that established the position of a note relative to all the other notes.

A note could have an identifier as simple as the number “14”, indicating that it should be placed after the note “13” as a subsequent thought. When placing a new note, if it elaborates deeper on the ideas of the note “13”, it could form a branch, called “13a”. New notes on the same topic could either continue building on the branch, with the code “13b”, or go a new level deeper with the code “13a1”. It could get as deep as “54e7b2”, for example. Nowadays, we have apps that facilitate the connections, but the idea remains.

notes.title: You can distill a note using progressive summarization
notes.html:
Tiago Forte created a method to distilling a note in his knowledge system, the Second Brain, called "progressive summarization". First, you read a long note and bold the main ideas. Second, you read the bold points and highlight only the essential part of each idea. Last, you write a summary of the highlights, that will represent the distilled version of the long note. You can place that summary on the top of the note, so whenever you come back to the note, you will be able to understand

notes.title: You can organize your notes in folders that represent projects, areas, resources, and archive
notes.html:
Tiago Forte created a folder structure to organize notes on his knowledge system, the Second Brain. He calls this method "PARA", acronym for projects, areas, resources, and archive. Projects represent short term efforts you are working with a start and end date. Areas represent long term functions you have in your life, like health, finances, family. Resources represent topics you are interested in understanding. Archive is a place for everything else, including finished projects, areas that stopped being relevant, and resources that you are not sure that will be useful. Whenever you create a new note, you should ask yourself where that note will be useful first: at a project level? If not, at an area level? If not, at a resource level? If not, keep it in the archive folder.
